title: Tech Competence
pub: LawSites / LawNext (living tracker page, maintained since 2015)
author: Robert Ambrogi

dom.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s competence and continuing-reassessment framework by supplying its pre-generative-AI regulatory foundation: technology competence had already diffused across many jurisdictions and required lawyers to understand technology’s benefits and risks. It materially adds historical and jurisdictional context, but does not directly address substantive verification burdens, confidentiality controls, or whether checking consumes efficiency gains.
qs: The opinion expressly cites the ABA’s Comment 8 and states:  Maintaining learning and skill consistent with an attorney’s duty of competence includes “keeping abreast of changes in the law and its practice, including the benefits and risks associated with technology.”  If you know of other states I have missed, please let me know.

kp.k: ABA incorporated technology into its competence guidance in 2012
kp.d: Ambrogi reports that the ABA House of Delegates amended Comment 8 to Model Rule 1.1 in 2012, clarifying that professional competence encompasses technology as well as law and legal practice. The quoted comment connects awareness of relevant technology’s benefits and risks with continuing study, education and applicable CLE requirements; it does not prescribe a generative-AI-specific training programme.
qs: More specifically, the ABA’s House of Delegates voted to amend Comment 8 to Model Rule 1.1, which pertains to competence, to read as follows:
including the benefits and risks associated with relevant technology
engage in continuing study and education and comply with all continuing legal education requirements to which the lawyer is subject.

kp.k: Jurisdictional adoption determines applicability, not ABA approval alone
kp.d: The author distinguishes ABA model guidance from jurisdiction-specific professional rules. States may adopt, reject or modify the Model Rules; the tracker explains that the relevant high court or rule-setting body must adopt the technology-competence duty before it applies to lawyers in that state.
qs: They provide guidance to the states in formulating their own rules of professional conduct. Each state is free to adopt, reject, ignore or modify the Model Rules.
For the duty of technology competence to apply to the lawyers in any given state, that state’s high court (or rule-setting body) would first have to adopt it.

kp.k: Tracker reports adoption across forty states and two jurisdictions
kp.d: The supplied 2025 tracker reports 40 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico, with jurisdiction-specific approval and effective dates. Adoption is distinct from commencement: D.C. approved its change April 7, 2025, effective upon approval, whereas Puerto Rico approved its change June 17, 2025, with effectiveness scheduled for January 1, 2026. The reported total therefore is not a count of duties already effective throughout 2025.
qs: On this page, I track the states that have formally adopted the revised comment to Rule 1.1. The total so far is 40 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico.
approved April 7, 2025
effective upon approval.
approved June 17, 2025
effective Jan. 1, 2026.

kp.k: Adopters vary in wording and placement
kp.d: The tracker explicitly identifies North Carolina’s variation, tying technology relevance to the lawyer’s practice, and directs readers to paragraph 5 of Montana’s Preamble. These entries qualify any reading of the tally as adoption of identical Comment 8 language in every jurisdiction. The supplied relevance note also cautions that descriptions of D.C. and Puerto Rico taking different or broader approaches come from linked post titles, rather than substantive explanations in the tracker.
qs: Note that the phrase adopted by N.C. varies slightly from the Model Rule:
with the technology relevant to the lawyer’s practice.
(see paragraph 5 under Preamble).
neither characterisation appears in the tracker's own prose, and neither post is held in this corpus.

kp.k: California opinion requires e-discovery competence or competent assistance
kp.d: Ambrogi reports that California Formal Opinion No. 2015-193 requires litigation attorneys either to possess e-discovery competence or associate with competent others, expressly citing ABA Comment 8. The living page contains an unresolved temporal inconsistency: its closing discussion describes California as not having formally adopted the change, while its jurisdiction list records approval on February 18, 2021, effective March 22, 2021.
qs: requires attorneys who represent clients in litigation either to be competent in e-discovery or associate with others who are competent.

California, while not having formally adopted the change to its rules of professional conduct, has issued an ethics opinion that expressly acknowledges a duty of lawyers to be competent in technology.
California, approved Feb. 18, 2021, effective March 22, 2021.

kp.k: Technology competence supplies background for AI-era regulatory responses
kp.d: The supplied project-relevance section frames the tracker as a historical foundation for later generative-AI guidance, judicial standing orders and CLE mandates, describing diffusion over thirteen years. This is the corpus’s contextual interpretation, not a tracker finding about AI’s effects on employment, legal-service quality or business models. The section classifies the page as practitioner-journalist reporting about primary rules, rather than primary legal authority itself.
qs: a comment-level duty diffusing state by state over thirteen years, with textual divergence among adopters
it is the base on which AI-era competence claims (state bar generative-AI guidance, judicial standing orders, CLE mandates) are being layered.
a practitioner-journalist's tracking page about primary rules, not the rules themselves.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ambrogi reports that technology competence has become an expressly recognised professional duty across many US jurisdictions; the tracker makes no AI-specific prediction.
pts.d: Ambrogi describes the ABA's 2012 amendment to Comment 8 to Model Rule 1.1 as clarifying that lawyers' competence extends to technology. He reports adoption in 40 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico. This is a claim about professional regulation of technology generally, not a claim that lawyers must adopt AI or that AI will change employment, pricing or service quality. The supplied 'Relevance to the project' section connects the tracker to AI-era competence requirements, but that contextual interpretation should not be attributed to Ambrogi.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of quoted professional guidance and a jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction adoption tracker with links to rules, orders and reporting.
pts.d: Ambrogi supplies the amended ABA comment and lists jurisdictional approval or effective dates, supported by links to primary regulatory materials and LawSites reporting. He also cites California's Formal Opinion No. 2015-193 concerning e-discovery competence. These are documentary and authority-based supports for regulatory adoption, not empirical evidence of AI performance or lawyers' actual competence. The supplied page contains a temporal inconsistency: its list records California's 2021 adoption, while a later paragraph still describes California as not having formally adopted the change.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The tracker traces adoption following the 2012 ABA amendment; applicability depends on jurisdictional action and effective dates.
pts.d: The supplied 2025 version includes D.C.'s April 7, 2025 approval, effective upon approval, and Puerto Rico's June 17, 2025 approval, effective January 1, 2026. Consequently, the reported adoption total is not necessarily a total of provisions already effective in 2025. Ambrogi explicitly distinguishes the ABA model from jurisdictional rules and notes that jurisdictions can modify the model. North Carolina's quoted wording ties technology relevance specifically to the lawyer's practice. No timeframe for AI-driven market change is offered.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The stated duty affects lawyers subject to adopting jurisdictions' rules, with a specific e-discovery example for litigators.
pts.d: The professional obligation concerns maintaining knowledge and skill about relevant technology's benefits and risks, alongside continuing study and applicable legal education requirements. Ambrogi's California example says litigators must possess e-discovery competence or associate with others who do. The tracker does not differentiate effects by firm size or business model, quantify client benefits, or impose an AI-specific training or use requirement.
